headline: Surgery opens the body to fix what can't be healed from outside
universal_truth: Some problems require direct intervention; working around obstacles sometimes means going through them
fun_facts: Ancient Egyptians performed surgeries over 4,000 years ago—including brain surgery
Before anesthesia in the 1840s, surgery meant being held down while fully conscious
Minimally invasive surgery can now be done through incisions smaller than a centimeter
discussion_questions: How did anesthesia change what surgery could accomplish?
What makes some surgeries routine and others risky?
How might surgery change in the future?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Surgery seems modern, but humans have cut into bodies for thousands of years. What changed isn't the idea but the execution: anesthesia to prevent pain, antiseptics to prevent infection, and precision to minimize damage. Ancient concept, modern refinement.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Opening a body is dangerous—infection, bleeding, shock. What breakthroughs transformed surgery from desperate last resort to routine procedure?

options.text: Anesthesia to prevent pain, antiseptics to prevent infection, and techniques to control bleeding
options.response: Yes. These three advances transformed surgery. Without pain, surgeons could take time. Without infection, patients survived. Without bleeding out, complex procedures became possible.
Tools improved, but the key advances were in pain control, infection prevention, and bleeding management...

q1.title: Anesthesia Revolution
q1.script: Before the 1840s, surgery meant enduring full consciousness while being cut open. Anesthesia changed everything—surgeons could work carefully instead of racing against unbearable pain. Patients survived operations that were previously fatal.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Anesthesia Revolution"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Germ Theory
q2.script: Until the 1860s, surgeons didn't wash hands between patients—infections killed more than the surgeries. Understanding that germs cause infection transformed surgery. Sterile technique made the operating room safe.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Minimally Invasive
q3.script: Modern surgery often uses tiny cameras and instruments through small incisions. Patients recover faster with less trauma. Robotic assistance provides precision beyond human hands. Surgery keeps becoming smaller, safer, and smarter.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Some problems require direct intervention. Surgery teaches that working around obstacles sometimes means going through them. When the body can't heal itself, we've learned to reach in and help.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 128. Tomorrow, we'll explore why clean matters—sanitation. Until then, appreciate that surgeries saving lives today were impossible just generations ago.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Medical Progress - Appreciate Advances
growTrack.learning_objective: Appreciate medical progress we take for granted
growTrack.activity: Think about any surgery you or someone you know has had. A century ago, the same procedure might have been impossible or deadly. Medical progress is real and remarkable. We live in an age of healing options our ancestors couldn't imagine.
